title: Cognitive dissonance in the placebo treatment of insomnia -- a pilot experiment.
journal: The British journal of medical psychology
abstract: Insomnia in 11 general hospital in-patients was treated by a placebo. The conditions of administration of the placebo were experimentally varied, and a hypothesis derived from Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory was tested. Consistent with this hypothesis, it was found that patients who were required to make meaningful decisions concerning their treatment derived significantly greater hypnotic (therapeutic) value from it than did patients whose treatment was simply administered to them and who were not required to make such decisions. The power of cognitive dissonance theory to explain the placebo effect, and the therapeutic potential of this approach are discussed.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of placebo administration (decision-making vs. passive) tested cognitive-dissonance mechanism and found differential placebo (hypnotic) benefit in insomnia patients, so placebo effect was the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Treated 11 hospitalized insomnia patients with a placebo while experimentally varying administration (decision-making vs. passive) and found those making meaningful decisions reported greater hypnotic benefit.
classification.key_finding: Patients required to make meaningful treatment decisions reported significantly greater hypnotic (placebo) benefit than patients given the placebo without choice.

title: Conditioned hypoglycemia.
journal: Journal of comparative and physiological psychology
abstract: An experiment was conducted to determine whether conditioned hypoglycemia would develop in rats that never became hypoglycemic on the conditioning trials. Rats were given saline, insulin, glucose, or glucose plus insulin as the unconditioned stimulus in a classical conditioning paradigm. It was found that a change of blood glucose need not occur on the conditioning trials in order to obtain successful conditioning of a hypoglycemic response; rather, an increase of insulin was all that was necessary. An explanation of conditioned hypoglycemia as the logical response of glucoregulatory centers of the central nervous system is proposed.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment tested classical conditioning of hypoglycemia (cue-induced physiological response), which is a mechanistic model of conditioned/placebo-like responses and thus meets inclusion criterion for mechanistic animal models of context/cue effects.

classification.summary: Found that rats could develop conditioned hypoglycemia via classical conditioning, driven by increases in insulin without overt hypoglycemia on conditioning trials.
classification.key_finding: Conditioned hypoglycemic responses were acquired in rats when insulin increased during conditioning, even without actual hypoglycemia on conditioning trials.

title: Principal aspects of the use of placebos.
abstract: After a brief historical review the author discusses the use of placebo in treatment and in the scientific evaluation of the efficacy of psychotropic drugs in double-blind studies. He also mentions its place in the elucidation of the personality structure and psychodynamics of so-called placebo reactors, as well as its importance in recent years for basic medical research.

screening.rationale: Narrative review of the use of placebos, trials, and placebo reactors so placebo is the main subject (placebo science review).

classification.summary: Reviewed the history and principal uses of placebos in treatment and psychotropic drug trials, discussing placebo responders and implications for research.

title: The effects of cerebral electric therapy (electrosleep) on anxiety, depression, and hostility in psychiatric patients.
journal: The Journal of nervous and mental disease
abstract: The effects of cerebral electric therapy (electrosleep) and placebo on self-ratings of anxiety, depression, and hostility were compared. No difference in the amount of improvement shown by the two groups appeared on any of the five measures employed, although a major placebo effect was evident on all of the criteria. The results argue against the use of electrosleep as a treatment for these symptoms except when it may be employed for its placebo value.

screening.rationale: Randomized controlled comparison of electrosleep versus placebo explicitly reported a major placebo effect on self-rated anxiety, depression and hostility, making the placebo response an analytic focus.

classification.summary: Compared electrosleep versus placebo in psychiatric patients and found no difference between groups but a large placebo-associated improvement on self-rated anxiety, depression, and hostility.
classification.key_finding: Found no superiority of electrosleep; a major placebo effect produced significant self-reported symptom improvement.

title: The power of suggestion: another examination of misattribution and insomnia.
journal: Journal of personality and social psychology
abstract: This experiment was conducted in an attempt to replicate and delimit the reverse placebo effect found by Storms and Nisbett in insomniacs. It was predicted that the reverse placebo effect would obtain when the pills' effects were described as affecting arousal (as in Storms and Nisbett's study) but that a direct suggestion effect would result when the pills were described as directly affecting sleep onset latency. Results indicated that direct suggestion effects obtained regardless of the focus of the instructions. The present study together with the findings of Kellogg and Baron call into question the reliability and clinical significance of the reverse placebo effect in the treatment of insomnia.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of verbal suggestion about inert pills' effects on sleep was the study's primary focus, testing placebo/suggestion effects in insomnia.

classification.summary: Conducted an experiment manipulating verbal suggestions about inert pills in insomniacs and found direct suggestion effects on sleep onset latency regardless of instruction focus.
classification.key_finding: Direct suggestion reduced sleep onset latency (subjective) regardless of whether pills were described as affecting arousal or sleep specifically.

title: Systematic desensitization and nonspecific treatment effects: a methodological evaluation.

screening.rationale: Narrative review in Psychological Bulletin explicitly evaluated nonspecific (placebo) treatment effects and methodology, meeting inclusion criterion 4 for reviews whose subject is placebo/nonspecific effects.

classification.summary: Reviewed methodological issues in systematic desensitization and nonspecific (placebo) treatment effects in psychotherapy research.

title: Disulfiram implantation: placebo, psychological deterrent, and pharmacological deterrent effects.
journal: The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science
abstract: In an effort to examine the placebo, psychological deterrent, and pharmacological deterrent effects associated with implanted disulfiram, subjects were given either disulfiram implants or sham operations. Ethanol challenges elicited no disulfiram-ethanol reactions (DERs), indicating that at the time of the challenge neither a pharmacological deterrent nor a placebo effect was operating. Of the patients who resumed drinking, only those with disulfiram implants experienced DERs. Sham operation subjects continued to drink after their first post-challenge drink; four of five disulfiram implant recidivists remained abstinent following their experience of a DER. It is concluded that the pharmacological deterrent effect of the disulfiram implant may have been underestimated in previous reports.

screening.rationale: Randomized/controlled trial contrasting disulfiram implants with sham operations explicitly tested placebo (psychological deterrent) and pharmacological deterrent effects.

classification.summary: Randomized controlled trial compared disulfiram implants to sham operations and found pharmacological disulfiram-ethanol reactions among implant recidivists, while sham subjects showed no such reactions and continued drinking.
classification.key_finding: Found evidence that pharmacological deterrent (disulfiram implant) produced aversive disulfiram-ethanol reactions that promoted abstinence in recidivists, whereas sham surgery produced no pharmacological or clear placebo deterrent at ethanol challenge.

title: Evoked potentials in hyperkinetic and normal children under certainty and uncertainty: a placebo and methylphenidate study.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a placebo and methylphenidate comparison with certainty/uncertainty manipulations but no abstract or methods available to confirm whether placebo/nocebo effects were an explicit focus or merely a control.

classification.summary: Reported evoked potentials in hyperkinetic and control children under certainty versus uncertainty during placebo and methylphenidate conditions; abstract and methods were unavailable to determine focus on placebo effects.

title: Issues at the clinical-research interface: placebo effect control groups.
journal: The Journal of nervous and mental disease
abstract: At the clinical-research interface, controls are a significant issue in group therapy evaluation. The authors describe and analyze their unique experience with placebo effect control groups conducted prior to brief, group psychotherapy for married couples. Procedures are outlined and participant reactions noted. Solicited ratings and spontaneous comments provide assessment data. The evidence suggests the feasibility of placebo effect control groups in the context studied. Proposed methodological refinements and clinical implications may be useful for future research efforts.

screening.rationale: Paper explicitly described and evaluated placebo-effect control groups for group psychotherapy, addressing placebo methodology at the clinical-research interface.

classification.summary: Described and evaluated the feasibility of placebo-effect control groups used before brief group psychotherapy for married couples, reporting participant ratings, comments, and methodological refinements.
classification.key_finding: Found that placebo-effect control groups were feasible in this psychotherapy context and proposed methodological refinements.

title: Morphine analgesic tolerance: its situation specificity supports a Pavlovian conditioning model.
abstract: Rats were made tolerant to morphine in either of two environments and then assessed for morphine-induced alteration of pain sensitivity in both environments. Analgesic tolerance was displayed when rats were tested in that environment in which they previously received morphine, but not in the alternative environment. The results indicate than an association between environmental cues and the systemic effects of morphine is crucial to tolerance development.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment demonstrated context-specific (Pavlovian) conditioning of morphine analgesic tolerance, addressing mechanisms of conditioned drug/context effects relevant to placebo/nocebo science (inclusion rule 3).

classification.summary: Found that morphine analgesic tolerance in rats was specific to the environment paired with prior morphine exposure, supporting a Pavlovian conditioning account of tolerance.
classification.key_finding: Morphine tolerance manifested when animals were tested in the environment previously paired with morphine but not in an alternative environment, indicating conditioned, context-specific tolerance.

title: Therapists' expectancies and treatment outcome: some overlooked factors.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title suggested the study examined therapists' expectancies and psychotherapy outcomes, but it was unclear whether placebo/nocebo effects were an explicit focus.

title: Letter: Continued need for placebos.
journal: The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science

title: An evaluation of the double-blind design in a study comparing lithium carbonate with placebo.
abstract: As part of a study of drug treatment of aggressive behavior to be reported separately, we have evaluated the double-blind procedure in a recently completed comparison of the efficacy of lithium carbonate versus placebo in modifying aggressive behavior in nonpsychotic incarcerated delinquents. We conclude that the side effects of lithium carbonate are sufficient to reveal the medication to most subjects receiving it. Thus, while the study staff could not identify lithium-receivers at better than chance levels, and while subjects who received placebo could not identify their medication at better than chance levels, subjects who received lithium could accurately identify it. On a weekly symptom check list there was no difference between lithium and placebo groups on average lithium target symptoms reported during 4-week pre- and postmedication control periods; however, lithium-receivers reported significantly more target symptoms every week medication was administered. Of 16 subjects who quit the study, 14 had received lithium and nearly all of those who gave reasons for quitting specified side effects, most often nausea. The methodological problems of using lithium in a double-blind design might be overcome by employing a "discontinuation" design, or, speculatively, a double-blind, cross-over design utilizing an "active placebo".

screening.rationale: Paper empirically evaluated the double-blind/placebo procedure and blinding validity (placebo science/methodology was the explicit focus), meeting inclusion rule 5.

classification.summary: Evaluated the double-blind procedure in a lithium-versus-placebo trial in incarcerated nonpsychotic delinquents and found lithium's side effects often unmasked treatment and led to higher reported symptoms and dropouts.
classification.key_finding: Lithium recipients could accurately identify their medication and reported more target symptoms and withdrawals due to side effects, indicating compromised blinding.

title: Acupuncture for chronic shoulder pain. An experimental study with attention to the role of placebo and hypnotic susceptibility.
abstract: One half of 42 subjects treated for painful shoulders received classic acupuncture, and one half received a placebo in which the needles did not penetrate the skin. Half of each of these groups was treated in a positive setting to encourage the subject, and half in a negative setting designed to keep encouragement at a minimum. All patients were independently rated for susceptibility to hypnosis. Although range of motion did not improve, the majority of patients reported significant improvement in shoulder discomfort to a blind evaluator after treatment; placebo and acupuncture groups did not differ in this respect, however. The positive and negative settings did not affect treatment outcome. In all groups, those who were not rated as highly susceptible to hypnosis tended to fail to achieve the highest levels of relief, but such differences were not statistically significant.

screening.rationale: Sham (nonpenetrating) acupuncture was compared with penetrating acupuncture and context (positive vs negative) was experimentally manipulated, with placebo/sham response and susceptibility examined as study aims.

classification.summary: Randomized trial compared penetrating versus nonpenetrating (sham) acupuncture and positive versus negative treatment setting in 42 patients with painful shoulders; most reported subjective improvement but acupuncture and sham did not differ and range of motion did not improve.
classification.key_finding: Majority reported significant subjective improvement in both acupuncture and sham groups, with no difference between groups (N=42).

title: Sequential withdrawal of stimulant drugs and use of behavior therapy with two hyperactive boys.
abstract: The separate and combined effects of stimulant drugs, placebos, and behavior therapy were investigated with two hyperactive boys. In each case, sequential replacement of drugs (Ritalin and Dexedrine) with placebos demonstrated placebo effects of the drugs; behavior therapy, alone and in combination with drugs, was effective in controlling hyperactive behaviors. Implications in regard to drugs as treatment of choice are discussed.

screening.rationale: Sequential replacement of active stimulants with placebos in two cases explicitly tested placebo effects as a primary focus (case series experimentally isolating placebo response/effect).

classification.summary: Reported two-case sequential drug-withdrawal replacements with placebo and behavior therapy, and found placebo effects when stimulants were substituted by inert pills while behavior therapy helped control hyperactivity.
classification.key_finding: Found that replacing stimulant medication with placebo produced observable placebo-related improvements in behavior in both boys while behavior therapy was effective alone and combined with drug treatment.

title: Personality factors and drug effects in a controlled study of cyclazocine.
abstract: This paper investigated the relationship between measurable personality factors and level of effects shown to cyclazocine and placebo in a controlled study. An attempt also was made through case analysis to examine the association between dynamic aspects of personality and adverse drug effect. Hysteria scores on the MMPI were found to be related significantly to self-reported effects under both the drug and placebo conditions. Clinical observations were examined retrospectively for three cases with adverse reactions and cited to support a dynamic theory that associated drug reactivity to personality factors.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly analyzed personality predictors of effects reported under both drug and placebo conditions, making placebo response an analytic focus (predictors of placebo effects).

classification.summary: Analyzed personality traits (MMPI hysteria) as predictors of self-reported effects under cyclazocine and placebo in a controlled clinical sample and found hysteria scores related to effects in both conditions.
classification.key_finding: Hysteria scores on the MMPI correlated significantly with self-reported effects under both drug and placebo conditions.

title: Role of expectancy set in the systematic desensitization of speech anxiety: an extension of prior research.
abstract: The influence of expectancy set with regard to therapy outcome on the effectiveness of systematic desensitization (SD) for reducing public speaking anxiety was investigated. The 7 Ss given a high expectancy set for favorable therapy outcome were informed about psychological research that indicates that SD is effective to reduce public speaking fears. SD was administered with the standard instructions to the 11 Ss given a neutral expectancy set. This expectancy manipulation did not require deception and perhaps could be used with actual SD therapy clients. As in previous research by Woy and Efran, the expectancy set manipulation significantly modified Ss' self-report of subjective perceptions of anxiety from pretreatment to posttreatment speeches, but did not affect overt behavioral or physiological indices of anxiety. Since subjective perceptions of anxiety responses are psychologically significant behaviors, these data suggest the importance of conveying a high expectation of improvement to SD and perhaps also to other types of therapy clients. SD sessions administered to small groups of clients on consecutive days, as in this study, appeared to be as effective to reduce speech anxiety as SD sessions administered to each client individually at 1-week intervals, as in the Woy and Efran study.

screening.rationale: The study experimentally manipulated expectancy set (verbal suggestion) as a moderator of systematic desensitization and analyzed its effects on subjective and objective anxiety measures, making placebo/expectation the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Manipulated expectancy set for systematic desensitization in people with public-speaking anxiety and found improved self-reported anxiety with high expectancy but no change in behavioral or physiological indices.
classification.key_finding: High-expectancy instructions significantly reduced self-reported speech anxiety from pre- to posttreatment, but did not affect behavioral or physiological measures.

title: Matching quality of agents employed in "double-blind" controlled clinical trials.
abstract: In an inquiry into the matching quality of preparations employed in double-blind controlled clinical trials, a panel of 4 observers studied 22 pairs of agents used in a sample of such trials, examining features which might make one preparation distinguishable from the other. 5 pairs of substances were an excellent match, being virtually indistinguishable, but in 7 pairs ther were obvious differences, detected by all 4 observers. The preparations used in cross-over studies were not specially well matched. Colour differences were most readily detected, followed by taste. The observers differed in their ability to detect differences between pairs of preparations, and 1 panel member was approximately 3 times more successful in doing so than another.

screening.rationale: Study empirically assessed matching quality of placebo/active preparations in double-blind trials, making placebo/blinding methodology the primary focus (placebo science).

classification.summary: Assessed the perceptual matching of 22 pairs of preparations used in double-blind trials and found many were distinguishable, with colour and taste most detectable and observer ability varying.

title: Who responds to sugar pills?
abstract: Among 288 cancer patients undergoing controlled trials of oral analgesics there were 112 who received 50% or greater pain relief from placebo formulations. Patients who responded to placebo had a greater response rate to active drugs. They also had a higher incidence of central nervous system side effects to placebo. Patient groups showing as increased placebo response included those with a high level of education, farmers, those with a professional occupation, women working outside the home, and patients who were widowed, separated, or divorced. Those resistant to placebo were patients with a low educational level, unskilled workers, housewives, married women without children, and smokers. It is theorized that placebo response is a type of autohypnosis phenomenon resulting from exaggerated oral-dependency needs. Particularly vulnerable to placebo effect is the very self-sufficient individual with heavy responsibilities who is thrust into the unaccustomed dependency of disabling illness.

screening.rationale: Paper explicitly analyzed and reported predictors and rates of placebo (sugar-pill) pain relief among cancer patients, making placebo response the analytic focus (placebo-arm analysis).

classification.summary: Analyzed placebo (sugar-pill) responses in cancer analgesic trials and found 112/288 patients had ≥50% pain relief, with demographic predictors of placebo response noted.
classification.key_finding: Found that 112 of 288 cancer patients had ≥50% pain relief on placebo; placebo responders were more likely to respond to active drugs and report CNS side effects.

title: Do placebos alter sleep?
abstract: Deliberate suggestion that an inert capsule was a sleeping pill was found not to influence subjective ratings of sleep quality or anxiety or the electrophysiologically recorded features of sleep in 10 volunteers aged 41-62 years.

screening.rationale: Study experimentally manipulated verbal suggestion that an inert capsule was a sleeping pill and measured subjective and electrophysiological sleep outcomes, directly testing a placebo effect on sleep.

classification.summary: Tested whether suggesting an inert capsule was a sleeping pill altered subjective sleep or electrophysiological sleep features in 10 middle-aged volunteers and found no effect.
classification.key_finding: No change in self-reported sleep quality or electrophysiological sleep measures after suggestion of an inert capsule as a sleeping pill.

title: Subjective ratings of sleep quality and anxiety after placebo, drug and a food drink.
abstract: Ten subjects (mean age 57 years) took part in a crossover study between a food drink and nitrazepam 5 mg. They rated their anxiety and sleep quality. On half the sleep laboratory nights during baseline periods subjects were given an inert pill which they were told would improve sleep. A comparison was made between the six pill and six non-pill nights for each subject. Subjective ratings revealed no significant difference attributable to the inert pill. Sleep quality was rated to have been improved during both late drug and early food drink administration. On early drug withdrawal sleep quality was rated worse than baseline.

screening.rationale: Within-subject comparison of inert pill versus non-pill nights directly tested a placebo effect on subjective sleep and anxiety ratings.

classification.summary: Conducted a crossover laboratory study in ten middle-aged adults and found no significant improvement in subjective sleep quality or anxiety attributable to an inert pill given on baseline nights.
classification.key_finding: No reliable placebo effect on subjective sleep quality or anxiety when comparing six pill versus six non-pill nights (N=10).

title: Credibility ratings for desensitization and pseudotherapy among moderately and mildly snake-avoidant college students.
abstract: Twenty moderately avoidant and 20 mildly avoidant Ss were chosen as though they were to participate in a snake-avoidance desensitization experiment. After relaxation training, Ss listened to a taped excerpt of either desensitization or pseudotherapy and responded to a 5-item questionnaire that assessed the credibility of the treatment. Mildly avoidant Ss rated desensitization as more credible than pseudotherapy. The implication of this finding is that a great many experimental studies of systematic desensitization have failed to control satisfactorily for the operation of expectancy effects and nonspecific forms of behavioral influence.

screening.rationale: Study experimentally manipulated therapeutic versus pseudotherapy tape and measured expectancy/credibility, addressing placebo-related expectancy and nonspecific effects in behavioral therapy research (placebo_science_other/expectation measurement).

classification.summary: Compared taped desensitization versus pseudotherapy in 40 snake-avoidant college students and measured treatment credibility; mildly avoidant participants rated desensitization as more credible than pseudotherapy.
classification.key_finding: Mildly avoidant participants rated desensitization as more credible than pseudotherapy, suggesting expectancy/nonspecific effects may confound desensitization studies.
